A celebrant is a person who officially leads or performs a ceremony. Think of them as the person who stands at the front and runs the event — not just someone who attends it or enjoys it, but the person responsible for making it happen in an official, formal way.

1. A Religious Officiant

In its oldest and most traditional sense, a celebrant is a member of the clergy (like a priest or bishop) who officially performs a religious ceremony or ritual — most commonly a religious service or sacred rite.

For example, at a Catholic Mass, the priest who leads the service and performs the sacrament is called the celebrant. He is not merely present — he is the one conducting the sacred act. This is the word's most precise, formal use, and in strict religious contexts, this is still what it means.

2. A Civil Celebrant

In modern everyday life, the word has grown broader. A civil celebrant is a professionally trained, legally authorised person who officiates at ceremonies that are not necessarily religious — such as:

  • Weddings (especially non-religious or interfaith ones)
  • Funerals and memorial services
  • Baby naming ceremonies
  • Vow renewal ceremonies

This type of celebrant is not a priest or religious leader. They are a trained professional — sometimes hired privately — whose job is to craft and conduct a meaningful, personalised ceremony for people who want something official and heartfelt, but outside of a religious setting. This use of the word is especially common in countries like Australia, the UK, New Zealand, and Ireland.

So in both meanings — religious and civil — the word points to the same essential role: the person officially in charge of performing the ceremony.

This is where many people get confused, so pay attention here.

A celebrant is not simply someone who is celebrating. A person dancing at a birthday party or cheering at a festival is not a celebrant — they are a celebrator (or simply someone "celebrating"). The two words look similar but mean different things.

Everyday confusionCorrect word

If your friend throws you a birthday party and everyone is having a great time, those happy guests are not celebrants — they are celebrators, or people celebrating. The celebrant would only be relevant if, say, someone stood up and formally officiated a toast, a ritual, or a structured ceremony as part of the event.

That said, you will sometimes see "celebrant" used loosely in newspapers or casual writing to mean "a person who is celebrating." This is considered informal and imprecise by careful writers and editors. If you want to sound accurate and educated, use "celebrant" only for the officiant — the person leading the ceremony.

Think of it this way: a celebrant is like a conductor of a ceremony, the way a conductor leads an orchestra. Just as the conductor is not simply listening to the music but is the one making it happen in a structured, official way — a celebrant is not simply present at a ceremony but is the one who gives it its official form and meaning.

  • At a church → the priest performing the Mass = the celebrant
  • At a beach wedding with no religious elements → the hired professional who officiates the vows = the celebrant
  • At a funeral run by a non-religious professional → that person = the celebrant

"The couple chose a civil celebrant rather than a priest, because they wanted a personalised ceremony that reflected their own values rather than a religious tradition."

Here, the celebrant is the professional who will stand before the couple and their guests, speak the official words, guide the ceremony from beginning to end, and make the marriage legally and ceremonially complete.

A celebrant is the person who officially performs or leads a ceremony — either a religious one (like a priest at a Mass) or a civil one (like a professional hired to officiate a wedding or funeral). It is not just someone who is celebrating.
